list.listitem: Dyspareunia is a clinical diagnosis based on a patient's report of painful intercourse; etiologies include organic, psychological, or mixed. C

A complete history, including sexual and psychosocial aspects, and careful pelvic examination with cotton swab testing and assessment of pelvic floor muscle tone form the basis for diagnosis of organic causes of dyspareunia. B
Treat specific causes of dyspareunia as appropriate. C
Consider referral for further evaluation of dyspareunia without an obvious cause. C
Cognitive behavioral therapy, electromyographic feedback, and surgery may be indicated in some cases. B

background.definition: Dyspareunia is recurrent or persistent genital pain experienced just before, during, or after sexual intercourse that causes distress or interpersonal difficulty. Dyspareunia is one of several sexual pain disorders along with vaginismus and noncoital sexual pain. Newer data suggest that dyspareunia is better classified as a pain syndrome as opposed to sexual dysfunction. This is an area of active investigation that holds potential for better delineation of etiologic factors, approach to diagnosis, and effective treatments.

list.listitem: In a systematic review of studies reporting adverse events after vaginal prolapse repairs using graft materials, the rate of dyspareunia based on 70 studies was 9.1%. There are similar rates of dyspareunia for synthetic and biological materials (low quality evidence).
Among 2,748 primiparous women who had resumed sexual intercourse by 6 months postpartum, 21.2% reported dyspareunia.

Given the sensitive nature of the topic and likely underreporting, the true prevalence of dyspareunia and its causes is unknown. Reported figures vary widely across studies as a result of definition used, population sampled, and manner in which data are collected.
Some studies suggest that dyspareunia affects 10% to 20% of US women.
Both men and women can experience dyspareunia, but it is much more common in women.
Overall: 9 to 750/1000 persons/year.
In the US, women stating that they experienced painful intercourse in the previous 12 months: 70/1000 women/year.
Prevalence of dyspareunia in an Australian population sample of women between the ages of 16 and 49 years who were still menstruating and were sexually active was 14.1%.

In a study of 6436 women who had given birth in Spain within the previous 12 months, 23.4 % (95% CI 22.3-24.8) reported dyspareunia. Associated risk factors were dyspareunia during pregnancy (adjusted prevalence ratio PR 2.1), having a history of episiotomy (PR 1.3), and breastfeeding (PR 1.2).

Twenty percent of a nationally representative sample of 1046 US women who reported sexual activity in the past 30 days had some degree of vulvar discomfort with sexual activity in the past 30 days. Correlations between the measures of vaginal lubrication, vaginal discomfort, and the 2 vulvar discomfort measures ranged from 0.46 to 0.77.
Only a small proportion of individuals with symptoms of sexual dysfunction, including dyspareunia, seek medical attention (20% of women, 10% of men).
Dyspareunia accounts for up to 15% of referrals to gynecologists.
The common causes of dyspareunia are listed in . In women younger than 50 years, vulvar vestibulitis is the most common cause; vulvovaginal atrophy is most common in women older than 50 years.
Other important causes to consider include vulvovaginitis, vaginismus, and vulvodynia.
Vaginal shortening following vaginal hysterectomy may cause dyspareunia.
Vaginal involvement in genital erosive lichen planus can also cause dyspareunia; vaginal synechiae and in some cases total vaginal obliteration can occur.

Deep dyspareunia was associated with bladder base pain which in turn was associated with presence of an abdominal wall trigger point and with pelvic floor tenderness in one study, suggesting a myofascial etiology and/or nervous system sensitization.
In cases without a readily-apparent physical cause, both physical and psychological factors are believed to play a role.

A theoretical model of one type of chronic dyspareunia (provoked vestibulodynia) was posed that incorporates stress-induced changes of pain amplification characteristic of chronic pain conditions in addition to sexual dysfunction arising from conscious pain avoidance, low self-acceptance, and/or fear-related inattention to sexual cues.

In a case series of 49 women breast cancer survivors with dyspareunia, all women were found to have vulvar vestibule tenderness but only one had significant vaginal mucosal tenderness despite vulvovaginal atrophy being present in 86%. The tenderness responded to topical lidocaine for most of these women.
Mechanisms of pain initiation and promulgation vary based on the etiology of dyspareunia in a specific patient.
In vulvar vestibulitis, pain is provoked by contact with the vestibule because of physiologic sensitivity or inflammation.

In women with vulvovaginal atrophy, postmenopausal decrease in estrogen levels leads to thinning of vulvar, vaginal, and urethral mucosa and decreased sexual lubrication. This delicate tissue may tear with sexual intercourse, leading to pain.
Vulvovaginitis resulting from Candida albicans or Trichomonas vaginalis may cause dyspareunia from local inflammation and edema of vulvar and vaginal mucosa.
Vaginismus is due to involuntary spasm of the perineal and levator muscles, resulting in inability to insert a penis, tampon, or digit into the vagina.

Vulvodynia refers to sharp, burning pain elicited by pressure anywhere on the vulva. This syndrome may be due to a spontaneous peripheral neuropathy; however, data are scant, and vulvodynia is currently considered a diagnosis of exclusion. One theory is that mast cell hyperactivity is responsible for the proliferation and sprouting of vestibular pain fibers.
Pain with intercourse can initiate from superficial (eg, vulva, introitus, hymenal ring) or deep pelvic structures (eg, uterus, uterosacral ligaments, ovaries, bladder; see ).

Women can have both types of dyspareunia; in one study, 66 of 150 women with superficial dyspareunia due to provoked vestibulodynia had concurrent deep dyspareunia. Among women with both conditions, endometriosis or interstitial cystitis was believed to be contributory and these women experienced more depression and more severe dyspareunia symptoms.

A new hypothesis for some cases of chronic dyspareunia is mast cell activation syndrome (chronic inappropriate mast cell activation resulting in chronic multisystem inflammation with or without allergic symptoms). The authors of this paper reported 5 women with chronic dyspareunia who responded to mast cell-targeted treatment.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Intrapartum second- or third degree tear
Big or medium problem at 1 month with perineal pain (6-month PP)

list.listitem: In a Cochrane review, a subgroup analysis demonstrated a reduction in dyspareunia by participants in the groups that had continuous suturing for all layers (vagina, perineal muscles and skin) for their episiotomy closure or repair of second-degree tear (RR 0.83; 95% CI, 0.70-0.98). Type of episiotomy (midline, mediolateral, or lateral) in one case series did not influence the presence of dyspareunia which was reported in 33/179 women (18.4%).

In a small underpowered RCT of 60 women following posterior colporrhaphy for prolapse, there were no significant differences in rates of de novo dyspareunia for women using vaginal dilators compared to control women (12.5% vs. 3.8% for control women).
The many potential etiologies of dyspareunia make diagnosis difficult. C
A complete history and physical examination, with the addition of the cotton swab test and assessment of pelvic floor musculature, are the most effective diagnostic tools. B

Ask whether pain is lifelong or more recently acquired, situational or generalized to all sexual partners. For lifelong pain consider vaginismus, inadequate lubrication or arousal, hymenal abnormalities, or phobic response to sexual activity. Acquired pain should prompt evaluation for infection, vulvar vestibulitis, psychological cause, or issues related to a new partner; situational pain indicates difficulty with a particular partner or sex act.

Ask whether pain is superficial or deep. Entry pain is common in vaginismus and inadequate lubrication but can be present in vulvar vestibulitis, vulvodynia, vulvovaginal atrophy, and UTI. Deep pain can be caused by endometriosis, pelvic adhesions, adnexal pathology, PID, cervicitis, endometritis, or uterine leiomyomata.
Location of pain at the introitus, vagina, or deeper pelvic structures and coital and postcoital timing of the onset of pain are the strongest predictors of dyspareunia with an organic etiology.

An educational gynecologic examination in which the patient observes the actions of the examiner in a mirror while the examiner instructs the patient in normal appearance and function of the genital structures is recommended.

The pelvic examination should include evaluation of the architecture and integrity of external genitalia and vaginal mucosa; assessment for vaginitis and pelvic infection with appropriate tests; and bimanual examination of the cervix, uterus, and ovaries.

In women who report entry pain, the vestibule should be palpated with a cotton swab in a clockwise fashion in an effort to recreate the painful sensation (Q-tip test). A positive test frequently indicates vulvar vestibulitis.

For women complaining of difficulty with vaginal penetration, evaluation of tone of pelvic floor muscles is of some value. A single, lubricated digit should be inserted into the vagina with palpation of the lateral levator muscles, pelvic floor, and vaginal walls. Hypertonicity, spasm, or tenderness can indicate vaginismus.

For women with suspected pelvic infection, measurement of vaginal pH, wet mount to evaluate cervical discharge for WBCs, Trichomonas vaginalis or Candida albicans, and cervical cultures for gonorrhea or chlamydia should be gathered.
The diagnosis of dyspareunia is clinical, based on the report of genital pain during intercourse regardless of clinical findings.
A patient's history will assist the provider in identifying possible medical or gynecologic causes and define the patient's sexual problems and their influence on sexual function.
The physical examination is focused on localizing the site of pain, assessing infection, and educating the patient regarding normal anatomy and sexual functioning.

The examination can be deferred at the first visit depending on patient comfort. For others, the woman should be reassured that she has control over the procedure and that her personal boundaries will be respected.

Consider referral for women for whom an organic cause is not apparent on history and physical examination; a multidisciplinary assessment of possible psychological factors or involvement of a physical therapist, particularly to assess pelvic muscle tone, can be helpful.
Dyspareunia is frequently multifactorial and may necessitate a multidisciplinary approach to treatment. B

Women with identified causes of dyspareunia (eg, infections, vulvovaginal atrophy, endometriosis, pelvic adhesions, uterine leiomyomata, and adnexal pathology) should be offered specific curative treatment. C
Short-term cognitive behavioral therapy, electromyographic feedback, and surgery have been shown to improve symptoms in women with dyspareunia. B
Infections (eg, vulvovaginitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, UTI) should be treated immediately based on the most recent CDC recommendations. Most women's symptoms resolve when inflammation improves.

Topical triamcinolone ointment was found in one retrospective study to resolve dyspareunia in just under half of women with lichen sclerosis who reported this symptom (dyspareunia was reported by 17 of the 34 women [55%]).

Vulvovaginal atrophy can be treated with topical vaginal estrogen; 80% to 90% of women report marked improvement in symptoms with use of estrogen cream, the estrogen-releasing vaginal ring, or estrogen tablets administered per vagina. In a recent systematic review, vaginal estrogens were uniformly more effective than placebo and more effective than non-hormonal moisturizers among women with two or more symptoms of vulvovaginal atrophy but not among those with a single or minor symptoms.

In one small placebo-controlled RCT, a selective estrogen receptor modulator (ospemifene at 60 mg daily) was effective in the treatment of vaginal dryness and dyspareunia. Adverse effects reported at 52 weeks in one study of 301 women included only hot flashes in 10%, leading to discontinuation for 2% of patients, and a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction in a patient with pre-existing cardiac disease.

Endometriosis can be treated medically with NSAIDs, low-dose combination oral contraceptives, progestin-only contraceptives, or gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist analogues. All drug treatments are equally effective (80%-90%).
Topical therapies for vulvar vestibulitis and vulvodynia (eg, fluconazole, cromolyn, and topical anesthetics) are no more effective than placebo in treating symptoms.

However, in an RCT of 46 breast cancer survivors with vulvovaginal atrophy and dyspareunia, women randomized to application of liquid lidocaine compresses to the vulvar vestibule before penetration vs. saline reported less pain with intercourse. After open-label lidocaine use, 37 (90%) of 41 reported comfortable penetration and no partners reported penile numbness.

Tricyclic antidepressants, venlafaxine, and anticonvulsants (eg, carbamazepine ) have shown little effect in treatment of these conditions. This may be confounded by the fact that 20% to 30% of patients with vulvar vestibulitis and vulvodynia improve without treatment or with placebo. In a cross-over study, lysate skin cream containing human cytokines was more effective than placebo cream in reducing focal redness and dyspareunia.

However, results of a recent RCT of 66 women with a history of vulvodynia suggest possible benefit of gabapentin over placebo for the areas of sexual desire, arousal, and satisfaction but not in orgasm, lubrication, or pain.

In an RCT of 40 women with severe, localized provoked vulvodynia, self-administered subcutaneous enoxaparin over 90 days significantly reduced vestibular sensitivity vs. placebo injections. In addition, 7 women in the enoxaparin group vs. 3 control women had nearly painless intercourse at study end. On biopsy, there was a reduction in intraepithelial free nerve fibers in women in the enoxaparin group vs. placebo.

Botulinum toxin injections into pelvic floor musculature have been shown to reduce dyspareunia in women with pelvic floor spasm significantly more than placebo in small randomized trials; use is still largely experimental. Authors of a systematic review of 9 studies and one unpublished found a significant reduction in patient-reported pain scores at 6 weeks after botulinum toxin injection (mean difference 20.3; 95% CI 11.7-28.9) which persisted past 12 weeks.

When less invasive medical and behavioral therapies have failed, some women with vulvar vestibulitis are candidates for surgical intervention via vestibuloplasty, vestibulectomy, or perineoplasty. Women with acquired, as compared to lifelong, vulvar vestibulitis; women without concomitant vaginismus; women with a small area of affected vestibular tissue; women without involvement of Skene's glands; and women willing to have sex therapy have a better surgical prognosis.
Reported success rates of surgical intervention for vulvar vestibulitis exceed 60%; however, because of methodologic flaws, interpret this with caution.

In a case series of women with symptomatic labial adhesions due to vulvar lichen sclerosus or lichen planus, sharp dissection of adhesions and injection of anesthesia was performed followed by continued medical suppression therapy. At a mean 2-year follow-up, most women had no labial refusion and 8/18 women with dyspareunia had no pain and 9 had less pain with intercourse.
Laparoscopic laser ablation is successful for treating pain in women with endometriosis or pelvic adhesions refractory to medical management.
Women with a suspected diagnosis of uterine leiomyomata should be referred for possible uterine artery embolization or hysterectomy.
In a small case series of women with posthysterectomy dyspareunia and chronic pelvic pain, vaginal vault excision resulted in improvement in dyspareunia and quality of life.
Native tissue vaginal apical prolapse repair with anti-incontinence surgery resulted in improved rates of dyspareunia from 25% to 16% by 24 months, but de novo dyspareunia occurred in 10%.
In one small RCT of women with chlamydia cervicitis, the addition of vitamin C to antibiotics improved symptoms of discharge and dyspareunia.
Daily intravaginal dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) may be effective in improving dyspareunia due to vaginal atrophy in postmenopausal women, but its potential benefit over vaginal estrogen is unknown.

In an RCT of 36 women with vulvodynia, acupuncture vs. wait list reduced vulvar pain and dyspareunia but had no effect on sexual desire, sexual arousal, lubrication, ability to orgasm or sexual satisfaction.

Electromyographic biofeedback (ie, training in biofeedback using an electromyographic sensor during pelvic floor exercises to reduce instability and hypertonicity of pelvic muscles) significantly improves pain associated with vulvar vestibulitis. Several small randomized trials show complete resolution of pain in 24% to 52% of women.

In an RCT of 64 women with dyspareunia, compared to the wait-list control group, women randomized to receive electrotherapy, manual therapy, and pelvic floor muscle exercises had improved sexual function with a mean difference in the Female Sexual Function Index score of 51.05 (scoring ranges from 2 to 95) and mean difference in the visual analog scale score of 7.32.
Data are limited on use of ultrasound for treating perineal pain and dyspareunia; 1 of 2 placebo-controlled trials found reduced dyspareunia with ultrasound (OR 0.31; 95% CI, 0.11-0.84).

In a small case series of 45 women with postpartum dyspareunia, nearly all improved with weekly application of intravaginal transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS); at 8 months, all women were symptom free. Without a control group, however, it is impossible to know whether TENS was actually effective.

Cognitive behavioral therapy has been shown to reduce genital pain in 39% of women undergoing short-term interventions (8-12 sessions). Treatment typically involves alleviating anxiety, normalizing alternative forms of sexual activity, and desensitizing activities.

There is little evidence to support systematic desensitization therapy (ie, relaxation exercises coupled with gradual desensitization to vaginal touch and penetration) for women with dyspareunia and vaginismus. In a case series of infertile couples in India, 60 of 63 women with primary vaginismus treated with a simplified sensate focus technique had complete symptom resolution and pregnancy was achieved in 33.
Psychotherapy, sexual therapy, and couple education are all recommended for the treatment of dyspareunia without organic causes, but data are limited.

Hygienic measures (eg, avoiding douching, soap, and panty liners; wearing cotton underwear; toilet hygiene; sitz baths) are frequently recommended, particularly for vulvar vestibulitis, but with little supporting evidence.
For women breast-cancer survivors, a pH-balanced vaginal gel containing lactic acid was not superior to placebo (lactate-free gel) in improving dyspareunia or sexual function.
Women with an organic cause of their painful intercourse requiring specialist care should be referred for definitive treatment.
For women without an identifiable cause of dyspareunia, referral to a psychologist, sexologist, or a multidisciplinary team trained to assess sexual pain is warranted.
Natural history of dyspareunia is poorly documented and largely unknown. C
20% to 30% of patients with vulvar vestibulitis and vulvodynia improve without treatment. C
Successfully treated women can go on to have healthy, pleasurable sexual relationships. C
